lessonTitle: Patents, Designs, Copyright and Trade Secrets

blocks.text: A company develops an electric scooter. Its folding mechanism is a new mechanical idea, the frame has a distinctive profile, the firmware and CAD files took two years to write, and the welding-and-ageing sequence that gives the frame its stiffness is known only to three people. Each of these four assets needs a different kind of legal protection, and choosing the wrong one can leave the most valuable asset unprotected.

blocks.markdown: Intellectual property (IP) rights let a creator or owner control the use of an intangible asset. The main forms used in engineering protect different things: **what a product does** (patents), **how a product looks** (registered designs), **how something is expressed** (copyright), and **what is deliberately kept secret** (trade secrets). Rights are national or regional, so the exact rules vary; the principles below follow UK and European practice, which most jurisdictions resemble.

rows: A new technical solution (product or process)
Appearance: shape, lines, contours, surface decoration
Renewable, up to 25 years in the UK and EU
Original expression: drawings, text, code (not the idea)
Automatic on creation, no registration in UK
Typically author's life plus 70 years for literary works
No registration; reasonable steps to keep it secret
As long as secrecy is kept
blocks.caption: Main forms of IP compared (durations are typical and vary by country and type).

blocks.markdown: Two distinctions matter. First, **ideas versus expression**: copyright never protects an idea or a method of operation, only the way it is written or drawn; someone who writes their own code to do the same job does not infringe. Second, **disclosure versus secrecy**: a patent is a trade of public disclosure for a time-limited monopoly, whereas a trade secret is protected only while it remains secret, and it gives no protection against someone who independently discovers or legitimately reverse-engineers it.

blocks.title: Patentability criteria
blocks.text: In the UK and under the European Patent Convention an invention is patentable if it is (1) new (novel), (2) involves an inventive step, and (3) is capable of industrial application. Some subject matter, such as discoveries, scientific theories and programs for computers as such, is excluded.

items: **Novelty**: the invention is not part of the state of the art, meaning anything made available to the public anywhere, by any means, before the filing (priority) date. Your own paper or product launch counts against you.
**Inventive step**: the invention is not obvious to a person skilled in the art, in light of the prior art. Combining known features in a predictable way is usually obvious.
**Industrial applicability**: the invention can be made or used in some kind of industry; a machine that violates the laws of physics fails.

blocks.title: Applying the patent criteria
blocks.prompt: An engineer designs a quick-release hydraulic coupling in which a ball-lock sleeve locks automatically under pressure, using a feature not found in any existing coupling. She presented a drawing at a trade show two months ago and has not yet filed. Assess the criteria.

steps.text: Industrial applicability: the coupling can be manufactured and used on hydraulic equipment, so it is satisfied.
Inventive step: the pressure-actuated locking feature is not shown in the prior art and gives a new technical effect, so a skilled person would not find it obvious. A search must confirm this.

Novelty: the trade-show drawing was a public disclosure before the filing date. In many countries it destroys novelty unless a narrow grace period applies (the UK and EPC have almost none), so the claim to novelty is at serious risk.
Advice: file immediately, ask a patent attorney about the jurisdictions in which the disclosure may be excused, and in future file before any public disclosure.

blocks.answer: Applicability and inventive step may be met, but novelty is jeopardised by her own prior disclosure; she should seek advice at once.

blocks.markdown: Choosing protection means matching each feature to the right form. A single product can use several at once, and combining them is normal.

blocks.title: Matching protection to product features
blocks.prompt: For the scooter described in the hook, assign the best form of protection to each asset: the folding-hinge mechanism, the frame profile, the firmware and CAD files, and the ageing-and-welding schedule.

steps.text: Folding mechanism: a technical solution that can be examined and disclosed. Patent, if new and inventive.
Frame profile: the value is in appearance (shape and lines), not function. Registered design, plus unregistered design rights in some jurisdictions.
Firmware and CAD: the value is in the specific code and drawings. Copyright arises automatically and prevents copying; it will not stop others from writing different code to do the same job.

Ageing and welding schedule: a process that can be hidden inside the factory and that competitors cannot easily infer from the product. Trade secret, supported by confidentiality agreements. A patent would require publishing it.

blocks.answer: Hinge: patent. Frame profile: registered design. Firmware and CAD: copyright. Ageing and welding schedule: trade secret.

blocks.title: Disclosure can end rights
blocks.text: Publishing a paper, showing a drawing, or selling a product before filing can destroy patent novelty. Similarly, telling an outsider a trade secret without a confidentiality agreement may end its protection.

blocks.title: Ask three questions
blocks.text: For any feature ask: Is it a technical solution (patent), an appearance (design), an expression (copyright) or hidden know-how (trade secret)? Could a competitor discover it by inspecting or reverse-engineering the product? Can it be kept secret for as long as it is valuable?

points: Patents protect new technical solutions, registered designs protect appearance, copyright protects original expression and trade secrets protect confidential know-how.
A patentable invention must be novel, involve an inventive step and be capable of industrial application; prior public disclosure by the inventor can destroy novelty.
Match each product feature to the form that protects what is actually valuable, and combine forms where appropriate.

questions.stem: A company wants to stop competitors copying the distinctive curved outer shape of its new espresso-machine casing, which has no special function. Which right is most appropriate?

options.text: A patent for the casing's function
A registered design for its appearance
A trade secret for its dimensions
Copyright in the machine's operating principle

questions.correctOptionText: A registered design for its appearance

distractorRationale.a: The shape has no new technical function, so there is nothing to patent.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: registered designs protect the appearance of a product, including its shape and contours.
distractorRationale.c: The dimensions are visible on the sold product and cannot be kept secret.
distractorRationale.d: Copyright does not protect operating principles or methods.

questions.explanation: The value here lies in the visual appearance, which is what a registered design protects. Patents protect technical function, and secrecy is not possible for a visible shape.

questions.stem: What does copyright protect in a set of CAD drawings and control software for a pump?

options.text: The idea of the pump's operating principle
The original expression in the drawings and source code
Any pump that performs the same function
The manufacturing process, even if not written down

questions.correctOptionText: The original expression in the drawings and source code

distractorRationale.a: Ideas and principles are not protected by copyright.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: copyright protects the particular expression, so copying the drawings or code is infringement.
distractorRationale.c: A different design doing the same job is not covered.
distractorRationale.d: An unwritten process is not an expression; know-how is protected as a trade secret if kept confidential.

questions.explanation: Copyright covers original expression such as drawings and code. It does not give a monopoly over an idea or function, which is the territory of patents.

questions.stem: An inventor presents her new valve design at a public conference in March and files a patent application in June. Which criterion is most at risk?

options.text: Industrial applicability
Novelty
Patent term
Copyright registration

distractorRationale.a: The valve can plainly be used in industry.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: public disclosure before the filing date forms part of the prior art and can destroy novelty.
distractorRationale.c: Term is the length of protection, not a patentability criterion.
distractorRationale.d: Copyright arises automatically and is not the issue.

questions.explanation: Novelty is judged at the filing date against everything made available to the public before it. The inventor's own earlier presentation counts, even though she made it.

questions.stem: Which description best matches the inventive step requirement?

options.text: The invention has been built and tested
The invention would not be obvious to a person skilled in the art in light of the prior art
The invention is commercially profitable
The invention is different in colour from existing products

questions.correctOptionText: The invention would not be obvious to a person skilled in the art in light of the prior art

distractorRationale.a: Reduction to practice is not the test.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: an inventive step means the invention is not an obvious development of the prior art.
distractorRationale.c: Commercial success may be evidence of inventiveness, but it is not the definition.
distractorRationale.d: Trivial differences in appearance are not an inventive step.

questions.explanation: Inventive step asks whether a skilled person, knowing the prior art, would have arrived at the invention without inventive effort. Combining known features in an expected way generally fails the test.

questions.stem: A machine that claims to produce more energy than it consumes would normally fail the industrial applicability requirement, because it cannot work as described.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Industrial applicability requires that the invention can be made or used in industry. A claimed device that violates established physical laws cannot be made to work as claimed, so it fails this requirement.

questions.stem: A foundry has developed a specific cooling schedule for a casting that gives superior fatigue life. The schedule cannot be deduced from the finished parts and is known to only a few trusted employees. Which protection suits it best?

options.text: A registered design
A trade secret protected by confidentiality agreements
Copyright in the finished casting
No protection is possible

questions.correctOptionText: A trade secret protected by confidentiality agreements

distractorRationale.a: A schedule is not an appearance.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it is confidential know-how that is not visible in the product, so secrecy is practical and avoids publication.
distractorRationale.c: Copyright does not protect processes or know-how.
distractorRationale.d: Secrecy plus agreements gives practical protection.

questions.explanation: Process know-how that cannot be inferred from the product is the classic trade secret. A patent would require full public disclosure and expire, whereas secrecy can last indefinitely if maintained.

questions.stem: A start-up has a new sealing mechanism that works differently from all known seals, but the casing it sits in is an ordinary cylinder. Which statement about protection is most accurate?

options.text: The mechanism is the candidate for a patent; the cylindrical casing is unlikely to justify a registered design
The casing deserves a patent and the mechanism a design
Neither can be protected
Both should be kept as trade secrets because they are visible on the product

questions.correctOptionText: The mechanism is the candidate for a patent; the cylindrical casing is unlikely to justify a registered design

distractorRationale.a: Correct: protection should follow the value: new technical function for a patent, not an ordinary shape.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the roles of the two forms.
distractorRationale.c: The mechanism may satisfy the patent criteria.
distractorRationale.d: A visible mechanism can be reverse-engineered, so secrecy is a poor choice.

questions.explanation: Registered designs depend on novel and individual appearance, and an ordinary cylinder has little. The seal's new technical effect points to patent protection, subject to novelty and inventive step.

questions.stem: Compare patents, registered designs, copyright and trade secrets by what each protects, how the right is obtained and its main limitation.
markingGuide: Patent: new, inventive, industrially applicable technical solutions; obtained by application and examination; limited term and requires public disclosure
Registered design: appearance of a product (shape, lines); obtained by registration; protects look, not function
Copyright: original expression (drawings, code, text); arises automatically; does not protect ideas or functions
Trade secret: confidential commercial know-how; no registration, requires reasonable secrecy; lost if disclosed or independently discovered or reverse engineered
Each has distinct term and cost implications
Notes that a product can use several forms at once
questions.explanation: A strong answer provides a clear distinction on each of the three dimensions rather than listing definitions. The marker looks for the limitations as well as the strengths of each right.

questions.stem: A researcher designs a heat-exchanger plate with a novel channel geometry that increases heat transfer by 25% over known plates. The geometry is not found in a literature search, and the plate can be mass-produced by stamping. Discuss whether the three criteria for patentability are met, and what the researcher should do about disclosure before filing.
markingGuide: States the three criteria: novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability
Industrial applicability: plate can be manufactured and used in heat exchangers
Novelty: not in the prior art according to the search, but the search must be thorough and no prior public disclosure by the researcher
Inventive step: a 25% technical improvement not suggested by the prior art supports non-obviousness, but a skilled person's perspective must be considered
Advises not publishing or presenting before filing and using confidentiality agreements
Recommends consulting a patent attorney and filing an application
questions.explanation: The answer should apply each criterion to the facts and not only state them. Marks are awarded for noting that early disclosure by the inventor would jeopardise novelty.

questions.stem: A company launches a cordless hedge trimmer. List five features of the product, including at least one appearance feature, one technical mechanism, one piece of software or documentation and one piece of confidential know-how, and say which form of IP protection best suits each, with a reason.
markingGuide: Technical mechanism, such as a blade-drive linkage: patent if new and inventive, with reasons
Appearance feature, such as the body shape and handle: registered design
Software or documentation: copyright, arising automatically on the expression
Confidential know-how, such as a battery-pack assembly process not visible in the product: trade secret
A fifth feature with correct form and reason (for example brand name as a trade mark, noting this is a further right)
Reasons link the choice to what is valuable and whether the feature can be kept secret or reverse-engineered
questions.explanation: The answer should justify each choice rather than just name it. A good response notes that visible features cannot be kept secret and that disclosure is the price of a patent.
